title: WHY DOES JESUS STILL PURSUE PEOPLE TRAPPED IN LUST?
paragraphs: WHY DOES JESUS STILL PURSUE PEOPLE TRAPPED IN LUST?

Because the Savior who sees what you delete, what you hide, what you replay, what you fantasize about, and what you swear will never happen again… is still standing at the door of your shame—not to help you manage your chains, but to break them.
There is a particular kind of silence that comes after lust.
Before it, there is anticipation.
During it, there is escape.
After it…
silence.
The screen goes dark.
The browser closes.
The message gets deleted.
The fantasy ends.
The body settles down.
And suddenly you are left alone with the person you were trying not to think about.
You.
Maybe you have whispered, “God, forgive me,” so many times that the words almost embarrass you now.
Maybe you meant it every time.
Maybe you cried.
Maybe you deleted the app.
Maybe you blocked the person.
Maybe you promised Jesus, “Never again.”
Then three days later…
again.
Or three hours later.
Again.
And eventually the question changes.
At first you asked, “How do I stop?”
Then you started asking something darker:
“Why would Jesus still want me?”
That question is where this story begins.
Because lust does something beyond tempting the body. When repeatedly welcomed and fed, it begins teaching the soul a theology of shame.
It tells you that because you keep returning to the same darkness, Jesus must eventually stop returning for you.
It whispers that grace probably has a limit.
That Christ forgives ordinary sinners, but not people who knew better.
Not people who prayed afterward and still went back.
Not pastors.
Not husbands.
Not wives.
Not teenagers raised in church.
Not the person secretly consuming pornography while publicly posting Bible verses.
Not the believer carrying sexual memories nobody knows about.
Not the person whose imagination has become a room they would be terrified to let anyone enter.
Lust says, “If people really knew you, they would leave.”
Then shame adds:
“And if Jesus really knew you, He would too.”
There is just one devastating problem with that lie.
Jesus already knows.
He knows everything.
And He is still calling you out of the darkness.
Jesus never treated lust casually. In fact, some of His strongest words confront it directly.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek text reads:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn…
Jesus says, in context, that the one who looks at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

The verb connected to this statement comes from ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, meaning to desire, long for, or covet. Desire itself is not automatically sinful in every biblical use of the word; context matters. But here Jesus is confronting desire deliberately turned toward sexual possession in the heart.
That means Jesus refuses the comfortable excuse:
“But I never actually touched anyone.”
Christ goes deeper.
Into the imagination.
Into intention.
Into what the eyes are being used to feed.
Into what you secretly rehearse.
Into the place nobody else can inspect.
Jesus takes sexual sin seriously precisely because He takes the human heart seriously.
He does not merely want your public behavior.
He wants you.
And that is why His pursuit of people trapped in lust should not be mistaken for approval of their lust.
Jesus does not pursue you because lust does not matter.
He pursues you because you matter too much to Him to leave you enslaved to it.
There is an enormous difference.
Modern culture often tells us that freedom means being able to satisfy desire.
Jesus offers something far more radical:
freedom from being ruled by desire.
The Gospel does not say, “Follow every appetite until you discover yourself.”
The Gospel says there is a King greater than your appetites.
There is a Savior greater than your urges.
There is a holiness greater than your fantasies.
And there is a joy deeper than the few minutes of counterfeit intimacy sin keeps selling you.
Think about how lust works.
It promises closeness while training you for isolation.
It promises satisfaction while increasing appetite.
It promises freedom while creating rituals you begin to feel powerless to resist.
It can reduce another human being—someone made in the image of God—to a body, an image, a fantasy, a source of stimulation.
Then, when it has taken what it wanted from you, shame walks through the door.
That pattern resembles what James describes:
“ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος…”
James 1:14 teaches that each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his or her own desire.
Then James describes the progression.
Desire conceives.
Sin is born.
Sin matures.
Death follows.
Notice how brutally honest Scripture is.
The Bible does not romanticize temptation.
It shows you where the road goes.
But Scripture also refuses to tell the repentant sinner that the road back to God has been permanently closed.
And maybe that is the part you have forgotten.
Your sin has a story.
But so does the blood of Jesus.
Your temptation has a voice.
But so does your Shepherd.
Your past has evidence against you.
But the cross has something greater.
A verdict purchased by Christ.
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about sins that included profound sexual brokenness. He did not pretend their former lives had been clean.
Then came three of the most beautiful words ever spoken over ruined people:
“καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε”
kai tauta tines ēte
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because Corinth had somehow produced morally flawless Christians.
Not because temptation disappeared overnight.
Not because everybody suddenly acquired a spotless history.
Paul continues:
“ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε, ἀλλὰ ἡγιάσθητε, ἀλλὰ ἐδικαιώθητε…”
“But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified…”
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That is 1 Corinthians 6:11.
Read it again if shame has been preaching louder than Scripture.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
The Gospel is not God pretending your filth was clean.
The Gospel is Christ cleansing sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
This is why Christianity cannot be reduced to “try harder.”
If willpower alone could resurrect dead hearts, Calvary would have been unnecessary.
Jesus did not come merely to give sexually broken people better habits.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
He came to forgive.
He came to cleanse.
He came to transform.
He came to make captives free.
And sometimes freedom begins with the most humiliating sentence a person can say:
“I need help.”
Maybe that sentence frightens you.
Because lust thrives in secrecy.
Pornography thrives there.
Affairs thrive there.
Emotional affairs thrive there.
Compulsive fantasy thrives there.
Secret messages thrive there.
The hidden folder thrives there.
The second account thrives there.
The relationship you keep calling “complicated” thrives there.
Sin loves rooms without windows.
Jesus keeps turning on the light.
Not because He enjoys humiliating you.
Because surgeons cannot remove what patients insist on hiding.
There is a moment in John 4 when Jesus meets a Samaritan woman beside a well.
The scene is already loaded with social tension. Jesus is a Jewish man speaking publicly with a Samaritan woman.
Then He touches the part of her history that could not remain hidden.
“Go, call your husband.”
She answers:
“I have no husband.”
Jesus tells her that she has had five husbands, and the man she currently has is not her husband.
Notice something remarkable.
Jesus knew this before He started the conversation.
He did not discover her history halfway through and suddenly reconsider whether she deserved His attention.
He approached the well already knowing.
He spoke to her already knowing.
He offered living water already knowing.
Truth did not cancel compassion.
Compassion did not cancel truth.
That is Jesus.
Some churches have failed people by giving them truth without tenderness.
Some corners of modern Christianity have failed people in the opposite direction by offering tenderness without repentance.
Jesus does neither.
He tells the truth that exposes us and offers the grace that can remake us.
The biblical word often translated “repent” is connected with the Greek μετάνοια — metanoia, repentance, a changed mind and turning that produces a changed direction.
Repentance is not merely feeling disgusting after sin.
You can hate how sin makes you feel and still love the sin itself.
You can cry after pornography and still protect access to it.
You can feel guilty about an affair and still keep the phone number.
You can ask God for deliverance while deliberately keeping the door unlocked for your next temptation.
Repentance gets practical.
Sometimes repentance looks like deleting something.
Sometimes it looks like ending contact.
Sometimes it looks like admitting the truth to your spouse.
Sometimes it means confessing to a mature, trustworthy Christian who can walk with you in accountability.
Sometimes it means putting serious boundaries around technology.
Sometimes it means refusing to take your phone into the room where you repeatedly fall.
Sometimes it means professional counseling when trauma, compulsive sexual behavior, relational wounds, or other deeper issues are involved.
Sometimes repentance means running.
Paul does not tell believers to negotiate with sexual immorality.
He writes:
pheugete tēn porneian
“Flee sexual immorality.”
1 Corinthians 6:18.
Flee.
There are battles Scripture tells you to stand and fight.
There are temptations Scripture tells you to run from.
You do not prove spiritual maturity by standing two inches from the fire and announcing how strong your faith is.
Sometimes holiness looks like running until the fire is behind you.
Joseph ran.
Paul says flee.
Jesus taught radical seriousness toward sin.
Yet here is what makes Christianity astonishing.
The command to flee sin is not a command to flee from Jesus.
Run from the pornography.
Run from the affair.
Run from the fantasy you deliberately cultivate.
Run from the messages.
Run from the secret account.
Run from the seductive situation.
Run from whatever repeatedly becomes your doorway back into slavery.
But while you are running from sin…
run toward Christ.
Some of you have been doing the opposite.
When you succeed spiritually, you pray.
When you fall, you disappear.
You skip Scripture.
You avoid worship.
You stop praying because you feel hypocritical.
You tell yourself you will return to Jesus after you have been “good” for a few days.
Do you realize what has happened?
You have accidentally turned your behavior into the price of admission to the presence of Christ.
But you do not clean yourself before coming to the One who cleanses you.
Hebrews tells us that Jesus is not a High Priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses. He was tempted, yet without sin.
Then Scripture gives frightened sinners an astonishing invitation:
Approach the throne of grace with confidence so that you may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
Not the throne of humiliation.
Not the throne of “I told you so.”
The throne of grace.
That does not make sin less serious.
It makes grace more astonishing.
And someone reading this needs to understand the difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says:
“This is destroying you. Bring it into the light. Come back.”
Condemnation says:
“You are disgusting. Hide from God.”
One leads toward repentance.
The other drives you deeper into isolation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα…”
Ouden ara nyn katakrima…
“There is therefore now no condemnation…”
for those who are in Christ Jesus.
No condemnation does not mean no correction.
No condemnation does not mean sin no longer matters.
It means those who belong to Christ do not live beneath the final judicial sentence their sins deserved, because Christ bore judgment for them.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the old pages never happened.
He rewrites everything by bringing redemption into a story sin appeared to have ruined.
This is the Gospel.
You sinned.
I sinned.
We have all fallen short of the glory of God.
Sin separates humanity from the holy God who created us.
And no amount of religious performance can erase our guilt.
So God did what we could never do.
Jesus Christ came.
The sinless Son of God entered our broken world.
He obeyed where we rebelled.
He remained pure where we became corrupted.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is not offered because sinners deserve another chance.
Forgiveness is offered because Jesus paid for it.
Grace is free to us.
It was unimaginably costly to Him.
So if you are trapped in lust, hear this carefully:
Jesus is not asking you to make peace with your chains.
He is calling you out of them.
He is not saying, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
He is saying, in effect, “Follow Me. Your sin will not be your master.”
You may stumble in the battle.
Sanctification can involve warfare.
Patterns built over years may require serious discipleship, accountability, confession, boundaries, renewed thinking, and repeated dependence upon the Holy Spirit.
But never confuse a battle with permission to surrender.
A Christian may experience temptation.
A Christian may struggle.
A Christian may fall and need repentance.
But the direction of discipleship is not making sin comfortable.
It is following Christ.
Maybe you fell last night.
Maybe five minutes ago.
Maybe this article found you immediately after you closed something you should never have opened.
Then do not waste the conviction.
Put the phone down.
Speak honestly to God.
No performance.
No religious speech.
Tell Him what happened.
Call sin what God calls it.
Ask forgiveness.
Turn.
Remove access where you can.
Seek trustworthy accountability.
And get back up.
Not because you are strong.
Because Christ is merciful.
There is something shame desperately does not want you to discover:
The moment you stop hiding is often the moment your chains begin losing their power.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your struggle. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
“Jesus, help me walk in purity.”

If Christ has already brought you through sexual bondage, pornography, an affair, destructive relationships, or years of secret shame, and it is appropriate for you to share, leave a testimony that points people to Jesus.
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need proof that repentance is possible and that grace does not merely forgive—it transforms.
And please hear this before shame twists even that invitation:
You do not owe strangers the intimate details of your past.
Wisdom matters.
Privacy matters.
Other people's dignity matters.
But you do not have to keep pretending you have never needed grace.
Neither have I.
Neither has any Christian.
We meet at the foot of the same cross.
Maybe you know somebody who needs this article.
Not somebody you want to embarrass.
Somebody you love.
Send it privately to someone who needs hope.
Come back and remember:
Christ is greater than the appetite.
Christ is greater than the memory.
Christ is greater than the algorithm.
Christ is greater than the image.
Christ is greater than the secret.
Christ is greater than the relapse.
Christ is greater than the shame.
Christ is greater.
If you want to help this work reach more people, sharing this article publicly is one meaningful way to do it.
Jesus Christ alone is Savior, and our allegiance belongs to Him.

But if this ministry genuinely strengthens your walk with Christ, financially supporting and sharing Gospel-centered work can be a practical way of helping that work continue reaching people who are hiding behind screens, smiles, church attendance, addictions, broken marriages, private battles, and unbearable shame.
This is bigger than merchandise.
Bigger than an algorithm.
Bigger than a page.
Bigger than numbers.
The goal is people encountering biblical truth and being pointed toward Jesus Christ.
So share the article.
Tag wisely.
Invite someone who has been drifting.
But before you leave, there is one last person we need to talk about.
The person you were when you began reading.
The one who wondered:
“Why does Jesus still pursue people trapped in lust?”
Now you know.
Not because lust is harmless.
Not because holiness is optional.
Not because Jesus has lowered His standard.
Not because grace gives us permission to remain chained.
Jesus pursues sinners because saving sinners is exactly why He came.
He exposes because He loves.
He corrects because He loves.
He calls us to repentance because He loves.
He forgives because His blood is sufficient.
He transforms because resurrection power does not merely improve graves.
It empties them.
So when temptation comes again—and it may—remember who is calling you.
When shame tells you to hide…
remember Adam hid.
Christ came looking for sinners.
When lust tells you, “Just one more time”…
remember what it told you last time.
When condemnation whispers, “Jesus must be finished with you”…
look toward the cross.
The cross is what sin cost.
The empty tomb is what Christ conquered.
You are not being invited to become comfortable with darkness.
You are being summoned into light.
Repent.
Believe.
Confess.
Flee sexual immorality.
Seek accountability.
Cut off what keeps feeding the fire.
Fill your mind with what is true.
Walk by the Spirit.
Keep returning to Scripture.
Keep looking to Christ.
And when you fall, do not build a house on the ground.
Get up.
Come back.
Because the final word over the repentant sinner does not belong to pornography.
It does not belong to adultery.
It does not belong to your browser history.
It does not belong to the person who used you.
It does not belong to the person you used.
It does not belong to the worst night of your life.
It does not belong to shame.
The final word belongs to Jesus.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you tonight is this:
Jesus did not walk into your darkness to decorate your chains—He came to lead you out of the prison.
